```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# load a few R packages
library(here)
library(knitr)

# for table fits
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
	library(flextable)
})

fit_flextable_to_page <- function(tbl, page_width = 6.5){
	
	ft_out <- tbl |> flextable::autofit()
	
	ft_width <- (dim(ft_out)$widths * page_width) /
		(flextable::flextable_dim(ft_out)$widths)
	
	ft_out <- flextable::width(ft_out, width = ft_width)
	
	return(ft_out)
}
```

# Reproducibility instructions

Our data and code are archived on GitHub (https://github.com/ahgroup/john-norovirus-antibody-kinetics-public) and Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19799472). To reproduce our results, first clone or download the GitHub repository. Once downloaded, open the `.Rproj` file in RStudio. We used the R package `targets` [@zotero-item-38674] to implement the analysis pipeline which can be executed in full by running `targets::tar_make()`. The pipeline automatically detects the number of cores on your device and runs in parallel, leaving two cores free. For reproducibility across devices, model fitting was parallelized adaptively based on available system resources. The total number of available CPU cores was determined while leaving two cores free, and each model was assigned approximately one quarter of the remaining cores (with at least one core per model) for MCMC sampling. This approach ensures that total core usage remains bounded while enabling efficient parallel computation across different computing environments. Note that parallel execution may be resource-intensive on personal computers; if you are in a limited computing environment, you can run sequentially by specifying `use_crew = FALSE`. However, running all Bayesian models sequentially may be very slow. You can visualize the workflow using `targets::tar_visnetwork()` and run only selected targets by passing a vector of target names to `tar_make()`, optionally using tidyselect helpers. Due to OS and file system differences, some targets may appear outdated even when up-to-date; this can be safely ignored. Note that not all model result files are included in the GitHub repository, as they exceed 10GB. To inspect or modify the Bayesian models, you will need to rerun the code.

Once you have cloned our repository, follow these instructions to reproduce our results.

1. Open the `john-norovirus-antibody-kinetics-public.Rproj` file in RStudio.
2. Once renv initializes, run the command renv::restore() in the console to begin installing the required packages. If you have issues at this stage you can also install the dependencies manually, but if you do not use renv or you use different package versions than we did, our code might not work for you.
3. If you want to run any steps that involve Bayesian models, you need to install cmdstanr following the cmdstanr quick start guide at this location: https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html. We used cmdstanr version 2.38.0 for this project [@jonah_gabry_cmdstanr_2025].
4.	Now you can run our pipeline by running `targets::tar_make()` in the console. If you would like to run only the main text results, run `targets::tar_make("reproduce_manuscript")` in the console. See the `_targets.R` file for further instructions and the full pipeline. If you are new to targets and want to learn more about how the pipeline works, we recommend reading the targets manual which can be found here: https://books.ropensci.org/targets/.

We conducted all analyses in R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31 ucrt) [@zotero-item-38678] in RStudio version 2026.01.0+392 [@zotero-item-38677]. The full pipeline, including supplementary analyses, took us approximately 17 hours to run. Reproducing only the main text analyses took us approximately 6 hours.

# Extended methods

## Model formulation

### Antibody induction model

The initial antibody response was modeled using a sigmoid function describing antibody concentration over time. The equation is given by

$$\mu(t) = \frac{P}{1+\exp(-G \cdot (t-K))}$$

where:

-   $P$ is the asymptotic amplitude of the induction term,

-   $G$ is the growth rate, and

-   $K$ is the inflection point at which the induction term reaches 50% of its asymptote.

To ensure biologically plausible trajectories, models were fit on the natural logarithmic scale, and parameters were exponentiated within the model to ensure positivity. To account for individual variation, the model for an individual $i$ at time $t$, denoted $\eta_{i,t}$, becomes:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \frac{\exp(p_i)}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_i)\cdot(t-\exp(k_i)))}$$

### Antibody decay models

We implemented two decay models: exponential and power-law. The exponential model assumes a constant rate of decay, whereas the power-law model allows the decay rate to slow over time, which may better reflect long-term immune memory dynamics. In both models, the decay parameter is denoted by $D$.

Exponential decay model: 

$$\exp(-D_1 \cdot t)$$

Power-law decay model: 

$$t^{-D_2}$$

Because the power-law function is undefined at $t=0$, we shift the time scale by one unit by replacing $t$ with $t+1$ to avoid singularities. As with the induction phase, the decay parameter is exponentiated to ensure positivity: $D = \exp(d_i)$. Individual variation is captured through subject-specific random effects on $d_i$.

### Full generative models

The full models were constructed as the product of the induction and decay components, expressed on the log scale. Let $\eta_{i,t}$ = $E[\text{log}(y_{i,t})]$ denote the expected log antibody level for individual $i$ at time $t$.

Exponential decay model:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \ln \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_1})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_1})\cdot(t-\exp(k_{i_1})))} \cdot \exp(-\exp(d_{i_1}) \cdot t) \right)$$

Power-law decay model:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \ln \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_2})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_2})\cdot((t+1)-\exp(k_{i_2})))} \cdot (t+1)^{-\exp(d_{i_2})} \right)$$

## Statistical model specification

Models were implemented in a Bayesian framework with weakly informative priors. All models assumed a Student-$t$ likelihood on the log scale to accommodate heavy-tailed biological variation and outliers. The degrees of freedom parameter $v$ was fixed at 4, and the residual scale parameter $\sigma$ was assigned a Half-Student-$t(3,0,2)$ prior.

$$\text{log}(y_{i,t}) \sim \text{Student}(v=4,\eta_{i,t},\sigma)$$

$$\sigma \sim \text{Half-Student}(3,0,2)$$


The expected antibody trajectory $\eta_{i,t}$ was defined as the product of the induction and decay components, with model-specific functional forms described below.

Dose level was included as a categorical predictor using a cell-means parameterization, allowing each dose group to have its own baseline trajectory parameters $p_{dose_i}, g_{dose_i}, k_{dose_i}, d_{dose_i}$. Individual-level variation was modeled using additive random effects on the latent parameter scale, denoted $p_{0,i}, g_{0,i}, k_{0,i}, d_{0,i}$. We assumed all random effects for a given parameter were drawn from the same underlying distribution.

Reflecting biological knowledge of antibody kinetics, weakly informative priors were assigned to latent model parameters: induction asymptote $p \sim \text{Normal}(7,2)$, growth rate $g \sim \text{Normal}(0,1.5)$, and inflection point $k \sim \text{Normal}(\log(10),1)$. We used separate priors for the exponential and power-law model decay parameters: $d_{exp} \sim \text{Normal}(-4,1.5)$ and $d_{pow} \sim \text{Normal}(-1,1.5)$. Random effect standard deviations were assigned Half-Student-$t(3,0,2)$ priors. All priors were assessed using prior and posterior predictive checks (@fig-prior-post-1 - @fig-prior-post-16).

### Exponential decay model

Time-series equation:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \ln \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_1})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_1})\cdot(t-\exp(k_{i_1})))} \cdot \exp(-\exp(d_{i_1}) \cdot t) \right)$$
Parameter definitions:

$$p_{i_1} = p_{0,i} + p_{1,dose_i}$$

$$g_{i_1} = g_{0,i} + g_{1,dose_i}$$

$$k_{i_1} = k_{0,i} + k_{1,dose_i}$$

$$d_{i_1} = d_{0,i} + d_{1,dose_i}$$

Random effects:

$$p_{0,i}, g_{0,i}, k_{0,i}, d_{0,i} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \gamma_{\cdot})$$

with group-level scales:

$$\gamma_p, \gamma_g, \gamma_k, \gamma_d \sim \text{Half-Student}(3,0,2)$$
Dose effects:

$$p_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(7,2)$$

$$g_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(0,1.5)$$

$$k_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(\log(10),1)$$

$$d_{1,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(-4,1.5)$$

### Power-law decay model

Time-series equation:

$$\eta_{i,t} = \ln \left( \frac{\exp(p_{i_2})}{1+\exp(-\exp(g_{i_2})\cdot((t+1)-\exp(k_{i_2})))} \cdot (t+1)^{-\exp(d_{i_2})} \right)$$

Parameter definitions:

$$p_{i_2} = p_{0,i} + p_{2,dose_i}$$

$$g_{i_2} = g_{0,i} + g_{2,dose_i}$$

$$k_{i_2} = k_{0,i} + k_{2,dose_i}$$

$$d_{i_2} = d_{0,i} + d_{2,dose_i}$$

Random effects:

$$p_{0,i}, g_{0,i}, k_{0,i}, d_{0,i} \sim \text{Normal}(0, \gamma_{\cdot})$$

with group-level scales:

$$\gamma_p, \gamma_g, \gamma_k, \gamma_d \sim \text{Half-Student}(3,0,2)$$

Dose effects:

$$p_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(7,2)$$

$$g_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(0,1.5)$$

$$k_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(\log(10),1)$$

$$d_{2,dose_i} \sim \text{Normal}(-1,1.5)$$

## Model implementation and computation

Models were implemented using the `brms` package [@burkner2021a], which uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) implemented via Stan, to draw posterior samples of the model parameters. Each model was fit with 3,000 iterations per chain, including 1,000 warm-up iterations and 2,000 post-warmup samples. With four parallel Markov chains, this resulted in a total of 8,000 posterior samples per model. An adaptive delta of 0.99 was used to reduce divergent transitions, and the maximum tree depth was set to 15, corresponding to a maximum of $2^{15}=32,768$ leapfrog steps per iteration. We used the default values for all other algorithm parameters.

### Censoring

Censoring rules were defined based on assay characteristics, prior literature, and observed clusters in the data. For HBGA measurements, the assay detection range was 25 to 3200. In the NI study, the lower limits of detection were 0.8 for IgA and 0.7 for IgG, whereas in the NV study they were 3.1 for IgA and 1.6 for IgG. Observations at or above the upper detection limit were treated as right-censored, and those at or below the lower detection limit were treated as interval-censored, with lower bounds set to $10^{-6}$ and upper bounds equal to the assay-specific detection limit. The lower bound of $10^{-6}$ was chosen to avoid undefined values on the log scale, as antibody levels are strictly positive. Censoring was directly incorporated into the likelihood using the censored-response functionality of the Bayesian models implemented in brms, allowing both right- and interval-censored observations to contribute appropriately to posterior inference. The number of censored observations by antibody, dose, and collection timepoint is reported for the NI study (@tbl-ni-cens-GI1-HBGA-4p8 - @tbl-ni-cens-GI1-IgG-4800) and the NV study (@tbl-nv-cens-GI1-HBGA-5 - @tbl-nv-cens-GII4-IgG-150).

## Model evaluation

A total of 16 models were fit, stratified by study, antibody, and decay function. Across analyses, posterior distributions were largely informed by the data, indicating that the weakly informative priors had minimal influence on the results (@fig-prior-post-1 - @fig-prior-post-16). Model performance was further supported by fitted-versus-observed plots (@fig-ni-fitted-observed, @fig-nv-fitted-observed), which demonstrated good agreement between predictions and data.

## Model comparison

We compared exponential and power-law decay models using approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO-CV) based on the expected log predictive density (ELPD) [@mcelreath2020; @sivula2025]. Model performance was assessed using the difference in expected log predictive density between models, defined as

$$\Delta ELPD = ELPD_{power-law} - ELPD_{exponential}$$

Positive values of $\Delta ELPD$ indicate better predictive performance of the power-law model relative to the exponential model.

We obtained an estimate of the standard error of $\Delta ELPD$ from the approximate LOO-CV procedure. In small sample settings, the uncertainty of $\Delta ELPD$ may be underestimated due to the instability of pointwise predictive contributions [@sivula2025]. To address this, we applied a conservative adjustment by inflating the standard error by a factor of two, following a heuristic for uncertainty quantification in small samples [@bengio2003]:

$$\tilde{\sigma}_{\Delta} = 2 \cdot SE(\Delta ELPD)$$

To quantify the probability that the power-law model has better predictive performance than the exponential model, we approximated the sampling distribution of $\Delta ELPD$ using a normal distribution:

$$\Delta ELPD \sim \text{Normal}(\mu_{\Delta}, \tilde{\sigma}^2_{\Delta})$$

where $\mu_{\Delta}$ is the estimated $\Delta ELPD$ and $\tilde{\sigma}_{\Delta}$ is the inflated standard error.

The probability that the power-law model is better than the exponential model is then given by:

$$P(\Delta ELPD > 0) = 1 - \Phi(0 | \mu_\Delta, \tilde{\sigma}_{\Delta})$$

Values of $P(\Delta ELPD > 0)$ close to 1 indicate strong support for the power-law model and values close to 0 indicate support for the exponential model.

## Modeling antibody kinetics

To estimate group-level antibody response trajectories over time for both the infection (NI) and vaccination (NV) studies, posterior predictions were generated over a finely spaced grid of time points. Time was discretized into two intervals: from day 0 to day 20 at 4-hour (1/6 day) intervals to capture early dynamics, and from day 20 to day 400 at daily intervals to capture long-term trajectories. Predictions were computed for all dose levels observed in the respective study.

Posterior predictions of the natural log-transformed antibody response were obtained using `brms::posterior_epred()` with `re_formula=NA`, excluding subject-specific random effects to generate population-level predictions. For each time point and dose, posterior summaries were computed using `brms::posterior_summary()` with robust estimation, returning 95% equal-tailed credible intervals (CIs).

Individual-level antibody response trajectories were estimated using the same framework, but retaining subject-specific random effects (`re_formula=NULL`), yielding conditional (subject-specific) trajectories.

## Derived antibody kinetics measures

We derived several antibody kinetics measures from the modeled trajectories, as illustrated in @fig-measures-schematic and described below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-measures-schematic
#| fig-cap: |
#|   [Schematic showing the derived antibody kinetic measures, including baseline, growth rate, peak titer, peak response, time of peak, decay rate, 1-year titer, and 1-year response.]{color="#FF2400"}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
knitr::include_graphics(here::here('results/figures/supplement/measures-schematic/measures-schematic.png'))
```

### Peak magnitude and time
For each posterior draw, the modeled antibody trajectory was evaluated to identify the maximum titer and the time at which it occurred. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were computed to summarize group-level uncertainty.

### Peak response relative to baseline
To assess the contribution of pre-existing antibodies, peak response relative to baseline was defined, for each posterior draw, as the difference between the estimated peak and baseline titers. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were used to summarize uncertainty.

### Early growth rate to peak
The rate of antibody increase following exposure was estimated for each posterior draw by identifying the time at which the modeled titer reached 50% of its peak value on the original scale, using linear interpolation between points on the prediction grid. The growth rate was then calculated as the slope of the log-transformed titer trajectory between the two grid points bracketing this value to capture the early exponential increase phase. Growth rates are reported per day, and posterior medians with 95% CIs summarize uncertainty.

### Antibody decay rate
Antibody waning was quantified as the change in modeled, natural log-transformed titer over one-day intervals centered at 60, 90, 180, and 365 days post-exposure. Multiple evaluation time points were used because the power-law model allows time-varying decay, whereas the exponential model assumes a constant decay rate.

### Predicted titer at 1 year
Predicted titer at one year was defined as the posterior-predicted antibody titer at day 365. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were computed across draws.

### Persistence relative to baseline at 1 year
To quantify antibody persistence relative to pre-existing immunity, predicted titer difference at one year was defined, for each posterior draw, as the difference between the predicted titer at day 365 and the baseline titer. Posterior medians and 95% CIs were summarized across draws.

## Pairwise dose comparisons of posterior kinetic measures

To quantify dose-dependent differences in antibody kinetics, we computed posterior probabilities of pairwise dose comparisons for each kinetic measure, antibody type, and study. For each group, we extracted posterior draws for each dose and formed all ordered pairs of doses. Draws were matched by MCMC iteration and pairs with missing values were excluded. For each dose pair (i, j), we calculated the posterior probability that the measure at dose i exceeded that at dose j as the proportion of paired draws in which the value at dose i was greater:

$$\text{Pr}(\text{dose}_i > \text{dose}_j) = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S}{\theta_i^{(s)} > \theta_j^{(s)}}$$

where $\theta^{(s)}$ denotes the $s$-th posterior draw and $S$ is the total number of paired draws.  Results are presented as heatmaps (@fig-ni-pow-measure-probabilities and @fig-nv-pow-measure-probabilities). We report each pairwise comparison in one direction only; the reverse follows as $P(dose_j > dose_i) = 1 − P(dose_i > dose_j)$, such that all pairwise information is retained.

### NV individual peak titers

The vaccine in the NV study used a two-dose vaccination regimen, with the second dose administered 28 days after the first dose. We initially hypothesized that antibody kinetics in the NV study would exhibit a distinct secondary growth phase or delayed peak following the booster dose. However, this pattern was not supported by the data. @fig-id-nv-model-zoom-1 to @fig-id-nv-model-zoom-5 show individual-level antibody trajectories from the NV study, showing observed data zoomed into the first 60 days post-vaccination. Day 28, corresponding to the second dose, is indicated by a dashed vertical line, and the observed peak titer for each individual is marked with a solid black point.

Visual inspection suggests that the majority of individuals reached their peak antibody titers before the second dose was administered. There was no consistent evidence of waning after the initial peak followed by a secondary rise after the booster dose. Because antibody kinetics in the NV study closely resembled those observed in the NI study, we applied the same model structure to both datasets. To allow for the possibility of delayed peak responses, wide priors were specified on the inflection point parameter ($K$), enabling the model to accommodate peaks occurring after the second dose if supported by the data.

It remains plausible that the second dose helps maintain antibody levels that might otherwise decline in its absence. Such an effect would be captured in the current model via the decay parameter ($D$), rather than through the emergence of a distinct secondary peak. Alternatively, it may indicate the need for a more flexible modeling approach in which the decay rate is allowed to vary over time, as in the power-law decay model, rather than assuming a constant exponential decline.

## Sensitivity analysis of censoring bounds

To account for censoring, observations below the assay’s lower limit of detection were treated as interval-censored. On the linear scale, the natural lower bound would be zero, but because antibody levels are modeled on a natural log scale, ln(0) is undefined. In the main analysis, we arbitrarily set a lower bound of $10^{-6}$ 

To assess the sensitivity of this choice, we performed additional analyses using a larger lower bound of $10^{-2}$ and a smaller lower bound of $10^{-14}$.

### Larger lower bound ($10^{-2}$)

The following table and figures correspond to Table 1 and Figures 2-4 in the main text, but were generated using a lower censoring bound of $10^{-2}$ for interval-censored observations (i.e., observations below the limit of detection).

## Sensitivity analysis of decay rate calculation

The power-law model assumes that antibody waning slows over time, so decay rate is inherently time-dependent. In the main text, we report decay rates calculated at day 90, defined as the rate of change from day 89 to day 90. As a sensitivity analysis, we also calculated decay rates at days 60, 180, and 365. The following figures present these additional estimates in the same context as the day-90 decay rates to evaluate whether the choice of time point influences the interpretation of antibody kinetics.

## Sensitivity analysis of antibody kinetics relative to baseline

@fig-ni-pow-measures-absolute and @fig-nv-pow-measures-absolute present peak and predicted one-year titers as kinetic measures, in the same context as Figures 3 and 4 of the main text, to assess the impact of baseline antibody levels on post-challenge or post-vaccination response kinetics. @fig-absolute-measures-vs and @fig-absolute-peak-decay-1year examine these measures within the same framework as Figures 5 and 6 of the main text. @fig-pow-gii4-absolute-measures-vs and @fig-pow-gii4-absolute-peak-decay-1year are analogous to @fig-pow-gii4-measures-vs and @fig-pow-gii4-peak-decay-1year but consider absolute measures.

In the NI study, baseline titers were generally balanced across dose groups for GI.1 HBGA, though the 4800 dose group had slightly lower IgA and IgG baselines. Peak response for HBGA decreased slightly with increasing dose, and this pattern was more pronounced when examining peak titers. Although the 4800 dose produced the largest IgA peak response, it had the smallest estimated peak titer. Similarly, while the 4800 dose had the largest predicted one-year response, absolute one-year titers were comparable across doses. IgG peak responses were similar across doses, but peak titers for the 4800 dose were lower than the other doses. These differences did not meaningfully affect one-year outcomes, as both response-based and absolute titers were similar across doses.

In the NV study, 50 and 150 doses had lower baseline GI.1 IgA, GII.4 IgA, and GII.4 IgG titers than the 5 and 15 doses. Although peak response and peak titer were qualitatively similar across doses, the 50 dose produced the largest one-year response but the smallest absolute one-year titer for these antibodies, again reflecting baseline differences.

Across studies, GI.1 baseline titers were comparable between infection and vaccination groups. NI groups showed slightly higher one-year HBGA responses than NV groups, particularly when we considered absolute titers. Importantly, absolute titers did not alter the relationships among growth, peak, decay, and one-year response: growth remained unassociated, peak remained positively associated, and decay remained negatively associated. Peak titer also remained positively associated with decay rate, highlighting the coupling between peak magnitude, waning, and one-year titers. In some dose groups, lower peak titers combined with slower waning resulted in comparatively higher one-year titers.

Absolute and baseline-relative measures introduced minor interpretational differences but our primary conclusions remained unchanged. Distinguishing between fold-rise above baseline and absolute antibody titer is important, as these measures reflect different aspects of immune response and potential protection.

Solid points represent population-level posterior estimates, with vertical lines indicating 95% CIs.
